items.title: The BEST prompt for AI agents I've heard over the last 12 months is ONLY 3 words, and it comes from someone who managed
items.content:
The BEST prompt for AI agents I've heard over the last 12 months is ONLY 3 words, and it comes from someone who managed multi-billion dollar P&Ls in AI, led a 100 person org at AWS, and now runs a brilliant AI workforce of 34 agents:

1. Her best prompt is just "do smart things"

She gives the agents all her context first, her calendar, email, Stripe, goals, and transcripts, then lets them decide what's worth doing. She realized every task still started as a thought in her own head, which meant the company could only ever be as good as what she remembered to ask for.

2. Her human team talks to her agents in Slack. She has a channel where a teammate can ask "did that financial services client reply to Ali's email," and the agents answer directly, so people stop waiting hours for her to get back to them. 

3. Since an AI agent costs almost nothing, she hired the person she'd never put on payroll. 

One does nothing but ask how to make everything ten times better. Another just watches the other agents work and flags where they get stuck.

4. She avoids old job titles, because the second you call one your CMO, you've rebuilt a 2015 company with robots. Most of her sub-agents run on cheaper, smaller models and do the job fine.

5. Run an AI watchdog instead of a dashboard. Point one at your Slack to catch two people doing the same work, at your calendar to flag conflicts, at your analytics to tell you what to post tomorrow. Almost nobody does this yet.

6. She keeps a daily "brain dump" that feeds the agents.

At the end of each day she dictates what's in her head that isn't written down anywhere, the stuff that only lived in a meeting or a Slack thread, and it goes into a wiki the agents read. That's how they get the context that email and calendar miss.

7. She uses a "last 30 days" research skill to spin up on anything fast. Before running a workshop for 200 execs in an industry she doesn't know, she fans out agents to scan and synthesize the last month of news, then walks in sounding like she's followed it for years.

That's my convo with @alliekmiller on @startupideaspod . Pretty much her biggest tips for using AI agents.

Full episode below. 

https://t.co/CukuBOXt9G

Happy building, I'm rooting for you.

18 two-word AI prompts I'm kind of obsessed with:

1) now what - great for when you've wrapped up a project or big push
items.content:
18 two-word AI prompts I'm kind of obsessed with:

1) now what - great for when you've wrapped up a project or big push and you still have energy and want AI to give you more

2) plz fix - usually accompanied with a screenshot flagging an issue or error or a DM with a bug report

3) do this - usually accompanied with a photo or a screenshot, if I see a great tweet that I want to implement, i'll just screenshot it and toss it to codex/claude

4) interview me - I'm a context hunter, and I want AI to keep pulling more context out of me that I didn't think to first give it, very helpful for tailoring responses or solutions

5) keep going! - I don't know, guys. I just find myself motivating my AI agents a lot more these days. Other versions of this include 'have fun' and 'I trust you'

6) elii elie - this is my shorthand for "explain it to me like I'm an intern" and "explain it to me like I'm an executive" and it's really helpful to get quick reframes if I'm stuck 

7) first principles? - sometimes I read an answer and think 'hmmm that's factually right, but it lacks heart and no one will care' and it's usually because the problem-solving wasn't upstream enough, this prompt helps reset that and reset assumptions

8) simulate it - love when AI runs scenarios, plans for edge cases, and visualizes it all into a dynamic interface for me, this is one of my favorites

9) challenge me - or 'challenge this', used when I desperately need a sparring partner and not a sycophantic kiss-ass :) helps to get a new perspective

10) da fuq? - Fable 5 took a different English class than I did because sometimes that model gives me five paragraphs of hyperdense phd-level info and I'm more lost than when we started

11) find leverage - show me the small moves that create disproportionate outcomes because I don’t always have time to optimize the 37 tiny things

12) hey simon - he's my AI chief of staff, and when I talk directly to him, he can route to and coordinate with the other 33 agents, this is the ultimate 'summoner'

13) spawn agents - any time I'm dealing with massive quantity (like tons of tasks or a lengthy spreadsheet or something), I aim for parallelization. dynamic workflows in claude is another great option 

14) automate this - many times, after a long conversation with AI, I realize that I will need to do that task a whole lot more. So I type something like 'automate this' or 'codify this' or 'schedule this' so it can become a repeatable pattern

15) remember this - any time I flag a mistake or critical context, I'm forcing the AI to log it into memory. It often does it automatically, but not always!

16) forecast impact - asks AI to play out the downstream consequences (including legal, PR, economic, political, team) of whatever I'm asking 

17) show receipts - I want to see solid sources, evidence, reasoning, so I can quickly call out issues (bad sources is a 'fail', and great sources are not an immediate 'pass')

18) girl bye - when AI loses its mind, and I need to get the heck out of there and start a new thread

items.content:
LLMs are not a path to human-level intelligence.
But they are very useful. 

Generative architectures that produce discrete tokens auto-regressively totally suck at modeling natural signals (like video or any high-dimension, continuous, noisy signal) and can't understand the real world.
That's why current AI assistant use separately-trained perception encoders (not LLMs). And that's why future AI systems will use non-generative architectures that operate in continuous representation space.

Agentic system cannot be made reliable and controllable without the ability to predict the consequences of their actions. That's why future intelligent systems will need world models with an ability to use these world models to plan.

Understood?

Data. 

So pick one niche. Pick one city. Track 100 businesses, not more.

Here's the part people miss: your first customer isn't the med spa owner.

Report, then dashboard, then API, then MCP tool. Agents pay per lookup once the rails are ready.

The catch is the filter. Valuable, repeatable, changing, fragmented, annoying. Annoying is where your margin lives.

Take one niche's messy internet and turn it into "clean fuel for agents."

items.title: Launch HN: Discovered Materials (YC P26) – AI agents to discover new materials
items.content:
Launch HN: Discovered Materials (YC P26) – AI agents to discover new materials Hey HN, we're Advaith and Akash from Discovered Materials ( https://discoveredmaterials.com/ ). We build AI agents that discover new materials for the semiconductor industry.

GPUs today have a heat problem. Nvidia & AMD are almost doubling the TDP (Thermal Design Power) in every chip they release - the H100 (released 2022) has a TDP of 700W, Blackwell (2024) gives out 1.2 kW and Rubin (2026) gives out at 2.3 kW of heat. This trend is expected to continue, and getting rid of this heat is one of the major reasons datacenters consume so much power and water today - they need it to keep chips cool during operation.

The amount of heat produced by a chip and its ability to dissipate it are both influenced by the materials used to make it. For example, we could reduce the energy per bit required to move data between logic and memory by 10-50x by 3D packaging chips (placing HBM memory stacks directly on top of logic chips, instead of placing them beside logic on a 2D circuit board). However, we're unable to do this today because the dielectric material used in HBM (such as SiO2) is a very poor thermal conductor, trapping heat between logic and memory and causing drastic temperature rise during operation. Similarly, there's many other materials in the GPU that are being re-evaluated today - 2 more examples are thermal interface materials and substrates. However, getting a new material into a fab takes years and hundreds of millions of dollars of research - the infamous "lab-to-fab valley of death".

At Discovered Materials, we're optimistic that AI agents can reduce the timeline and cost required to introduce new materials into semiconductor chips. We're seeing glimpses of this already - we tested 7 models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Kimi, and found that they're all able to computationally discover new materials that are dynamically stable and possess promising properties. This was surprising to us - it would generally take a PhD student a couple of weeks of work to discover the kind of materials that these models find over an 8 hour run!

However, computational discovery is the easy part. A material discovery is only valid if the material can be made and tested in a lab (As an example, graphene’s properties were predicted in 1947 but it was made for the first time in 2004). Today’s models are not good at coming up with synthesis recipes to make materials in a lab. Even if they do get better at it, we're uncertain about how much that will help - making a new material is a highly empirical process involving trial and error over many experiments. Human experts themselves cannot "one-shot" the task, but we expect that a highly capable model will reduce the number of experimental iterations required to make a new material. We’ve seen some evidence of this over the 3 months of our Y Combinator batch - we simulated, synthesized and tested thermal interface materials (TIMs) that match the performance of TIMs the world's largest chemical companies have guarded as trade secrets for over 20 years.

We’re releasing hundreds of hundreds of new materials discovered by frontier AI models, as well as our benchmark which measures model ability on material discovery here (also linked in the thread url): https://discoveredmaterials.com/research. It covers what we discuss above, as well as a variety of strange behavior that we observe from the models, such as Claude's propensity to reward hack or GPT-5.6 occasionally losing its mind after ~50M tokens.

Our business model: We aim to license and sell IP on the materials we discover, as well as the IP on how to make these materials. We're also exploring an alternate business model where we sell the harness+tools we use to discover materials to semiconductor and chemical companies, allowing them to discover materials on their own. We're leaning towards the latter to start, but we expect that we'll do both in the long run.

Our backstory: Akash has a PhD in Material Science from Stanford University, and has spent the last 11 years studying new materials for semiconductor chips. His work on new nanoscale interconnects was Stanford Engineering’s most popular story of 2025. Advaith studied AI at Carnegie Mellon and was a research engineer building video models and agents at Persona AI (acquired) and Luma Labs.

We are very interested in your opinion! The semiconductor industry is quite secretive, and your thoughts on the roadmap of the industry or the materials we should go after would be very helpful. We would also love to hear from people who have run experiments in labs - what can we learn from your experience doing empirical science?

items.content:
The best cash-flow services business right now is making a company readable to AI agents.

Here's why it works: you're not selling the future, you're "selling the screenshot."

You show a founder what AI says about their company today, and that becomes the whole sales deck.

Build it in five parts:
1) Vertical.
- Shopify apps, law firms, healthcare clinics, financial advisors, insurance brokers, home services.
- B2B SaaS is obvious, and too big. Go one layer down.

2) Prompts.
- Run 20 to 50 buyer intent prompts across the major AI tools.
- What's the best software for this use case? What does this company cost? What are the risks of choosing this vendor?

3) The reveal.
- Their site says $20 a month. The AI answer says $8 a month.
- Or it recommends the competitor because their docs are cleaner.
- Or the answer exists, buried in a PDF from 2002.

4) The fix.
- A clean llms.txt, a pricing page agents can parse, honest comparison pages, structured FAQs, schema markup, a change log.
- Plain language instead of "unlocking operational excellence."

5) The loop.
- Every month you rerun the same prompts and show what moved.
- $3,000 to $10,000 for the audit and cleanup. $10,000 to $20,000 for the larger B2B accounts.

The catch: this is a services business before it's a product.

Ten clients in one niche before you see it 

The same missing docs, the same unclear pricing, the same monthly report. That repetition is the software.

So pick the niche you already know, and run the prompts before you pitch anyone.

One of the best startup ideas right now is turning an expert's archive into an agent tool.

- Then charge $19 a month, or $50, or bundle it into the paid community, or license it to agencies. 
- The creator gets paid when the knowledge gets used instead of hoping someone sits through a pre-roll ad before a 47-minute interview from seven years ago.

Here's how to pitch the idea: "You have 300 videos about sales, we're turning them into a tool your audience uses to fix cold emails" 

So find the one job that expert gets asked about over and over. 

Build the tool around that one.

items.content:
What does a website look like when an agent is the customer?

Request. Price. Pay.

The old bargain of the internet:
- A search engine crawled your site
- It sent you a human
- You monetized that attention with ads, an email capture, a subscription, or an affiliate link

The agentic internet:
- An AI system reads your page
- It pulls the answer and hands it to the user
- The visit never happens, so the ad impression, the email, and the affiliate click go with it
A human won't pay a third of a cent to see a sauce recipe. I'd close the laptop and order tacos out of spite.

A machine doesn't care. Tiny and automatic, and the job gets done.

So Cloudflare built the rails: 
- Pay per crawl answers an AI crawler with a 402 payment required and a price, the crawler pays, then retries with proof of payment.

Same for a dataset, per lookup. Same for an API, per successful call. Same for an MCP tool call.

The request becomes the transaction.

The catch is deciding what to meter. Some things stay free because free buys distribution. Some stay blocked because they should stay private.

Ask what resource an agent needs badly enough, often enough, and reliably enough to pay for

items.content:
I absolutely hate AI writing. And my entire job is to write about AI. So I keep a file of the new em-dash to recognize AI writing instantly:

Everyone learned the em dash trick. 
AI is trained to not write with em dashes anymore. 
Now you can get accused of using AI if you write in perfectly structured sentences.

These are some of the dead giveaways of using AI:

1. "That's not X. That's Y."
"That's not compliance. That's stalling."
Say the second half only. "They're stalling."

2. Two short bits stuck together.
"Fast. Simple." "No fluff. Just answers."
Pick only one to write like a real person.

3. "Less a hammer, more a scalpel."
Visualizing two pictures with no advice. Directly say what to do instead.

4. Clapping for itself.
"And that matters." "That's the part everyone misses." "Which is exactly the point."
Delete them all. You lose nothing. I promise.

5. "It's the Excel of AI agents."
Only works if I know both things. Usually I don't.

6. Warming up before talking.
"Here's the thing." "Let me be clear." "The truth is."
Start one sentence later.

7. Always three things.
"Faster, cheaper, smarter."
Real life gives you two reasons. Or five. Never always three.

8. "5 to 10 minutes."
A range means you never did it. Just say 7 minutes.

9. The ending that repeats the whole post.
"In short…" "At the end of the day…"
Just stop typing. End on a high note.

Now that you know how AI writes. Here's how to actually stop AI from doing all nine:

Step 1. Type only these two words in your prompt.
Open chat & write: "Use ASD-STE100."

That's the writing standard for plane manuals. Short words, short sentences, because a confusing sentence there can kill someone. Claude already knows it. Those words remove 80% of the bad writing. Works on ChatGPT, Gemini & Grok too.

Step 2. Get the skill so you never type it again.

/ste gives you the first three but forgets about the fourth. This prompt puts it back on the track.

Copy the 9 patterns above into a file. Tell Claude to check every draft against it.

Then add a new line every time you spot one. Your file gets better every week. Mine certainly does.

Step 6. Start a new chat more often.

Buzz by Jack Dorsey just killed Slack.

→ If Hermes isn't auto-discovered inside Buzz, go to Settings → Add Runtimes to install it manually

Path 1: ACP (fastest, least control)

Buzz connects to agents through the Agent Client Protocol, the same standard Claude Code, Codex, and Goose already use. Hermes speaks ACP too, so it slots in as just another harness Buzz can call.

Auto-approves everything by default, no fine-grained tool authorization yet.

Path 2: Hermes Gateway plugin (the deep integration)

This is the real one. The Hermes Gateway ships as a bundled Buzz platform plugin, so Buzz gets treated as a full external platform instead of a chat window bolted on the side.

You get channels, DMs, threads, reactions, and scheduled task delivery, Hermes fully native inside your team's workspace.

Setup:

hermes gateway setup

Select Buzz from the platform list, then give it your relay URL (found in your community's hosted settings).

Path 3: Self-hosted, full control

Run the whole workspace yourself via the official Docker Compose bundle. Every message is a signed Nostr event, so you get a complete audit trail, and Hermes authenticates with its own cryptographic keypair, not a bot token.

What's actually solid right now:

→ All three paths are functional
→ Agent creation and channel membership work cleanly
→ Message signing and full audit trail
→ Desktop builds for macOS, Windows, Linux

What's still rough:

→ Mobile clients aren't complete yet
→ No fine-grained per-user tool permissions on Path 1, it auto-approves everything
→ Single relay per workspace, no multi-relay federation yet
→ Hosted onboarding has known bugs that can lock you out (check GitHub issues #2484, #2367 if it happens)

Once connected, your entire Hermes setup, config, credentials, memory, skills, lives inside a chat interface your whole team can actually use.

This is the prompt:

Higgsfield A single continuous 15-second shot. Extreme macro open on a single drop of water swelling at the lip of a matte-black faucet in a dim concrete studio. The drop releases and the camera falls with it in slow motion, tracking straight down. The instant it hits a still black pool, the impact blooms into a crown splash, individual droplets suspended mid-air catching a single warm rim light. 

The camera pushes through the splash and the water surface transforms into an aerial view of a vast misty mountain range at dawn, the ripples becoming rolling fog between dark peaks. Golden hour light breaks over the ridgeline, rays cutting through the mist. The camera keeps gliding forward over the peaks, revealing a lone winding river far below catching the sunrise like liquid gold.

The shot rises and the sky opens into a slow sweep of stars as day turns to night in one continuous motion, the Milky Way arcing overhead, its reflection shimmering in the river below.

Cinematic anamorphic lens, shallow depth of field, natural volumetric lighting, ultra-detailed water physics, realistic surface tension and refraction, film grain, 4K. 

Native audio: a single resonant water drop echo, rising ambient drone, wind moving across the peaks at the summit, and a deep cinematic swell as the stars appear. No music vocals, no dialogue.

2. GPT Image 2 — Blacksmith forge environment
Reference inputs:
Your shipyard image was used as the primary environment quality, lighting, scale, and composition reference.
Your blacksmith image was used as a secondary brushwork and handcrafted-world reference.

Use case: stylized-concept

Asset type: high-end environment concept-art reference for later AI-video generation

Input images:
Image 1 is the primary reference for exact environmental quality, portrait framing, monumental arched architecture, layered depth, broad painterly shapes, warm backlight, dark foreground framing, hanging lines, and restrained sepia palette.

Image 2 is secondary reference only for the handcrafted world, simplified brushwork, and material treatment.

Create a new blacksmith forge—not the shipyard shown in Image 1—and include no people.

Primary request:
Generate a monumental old blacksmith forge interior with soaring timber-and-stone arches, huge overhead roof ribs, suspended chains and pulley hooks, an elevated network of rough work platforms and beams, a large brick forge hearth, bellows, anvils, quenching tubs, hammer racks, long worktables, stacked iron billets, and small tool silhouettes.

Arrange the environment as strong separable architectural fragments that could later assemble around a rotating character.

Scene/backdrop:
Cavernous pre-industrial master forge, deep vertical space and layered work levels; broad open central aisle and clear floor area reserved for a full-body blacksmith.

Style/medium:
Premium painterly animation-production environment concept art; bold broad digital-gouache brushwork; large simplified value masses; atmospheric depth through layered warm light; rough expressive edges; sophisticated cinematic design; no comic outlines, no crosshatching, no photorealism.

Composition/framing:
Exact 4:5 portrait composition intended for 960 × 1200 px; low eye-level view down the open central forge aisle; massive dark arch shapes frame the left, right, and top edges; luminous workshop depth in the center; chains and hooks create thin vertical accents without closing the central character space.

Lighting/mood:
Powerful late-afternoon amber light pouring through tall high windows behind the forge; deep near-black foreground silhouettes; warm dusty shafts; quiet monumental craftsmanship; rugged, serious, mysterious.

Color palette:
Sepia, smoked umber, warm ochre, dusty beige, charcoal, aged wood brown, dark iron, very restrained ember orange.

Materials/textures:
Rough-hewn beams, soot-blackened stone, hammered iron, old brick, worn wood, dusty flagstone floor, cracked leather bellows.

Constraints:
Environment architecture only; no characters, people, faces or silhouettes; blacksmith forge equipment must be clearly identifiable; central open space must remain usable for a rotating full-body character; painterly concept-art finish matching the supplied reference quality; exact portrait 4:5 layout; no text, no letters, no logo, no watermark.

Avoid:
Copying ship hulls or shipyard-specific content from Image 1; comic-book ink; line-art crosshatching; crisp vector edges; clean modern factory; modern electric equipment; steampunk ornament overload; fantasy throne room; clutter blocking the central aisle; blue lighting; oversaturated fire; tiny busy detail everywhere.

items.content:
Everyone is talking about AI Agents. Few know how to build one.

You don't need to be an AI researcher or spend months learning machine learning.

You need a structured workflow.

Here's a practical framework to build your first AI agent in under 10 minutes:

1. Pick one repetitive task.
Don't start with "I want an AI assistant."
Start with a painful, repetitive workflow.

Examples:
• Summarizing meeting notes
• Responding to customer FAQs
• Qualifying sales leads
• Writing social media drafts
• Analyzing spreadsheets
• Reviewing resumes

The narrower the task, the better the AI performs.

2. Break the workflow into steps. Think like an operations manager.
Map:
Input → Actions → Decision → Output
Separate:
• Rule-based tasks
• Research tasks
• Human judgment
AI excels when the process is clearly defined.

3. Choose the right framework. You don't need to reinvent the wheel.

Popular options include:
• OpenAI Agents SDK
• LangGraph
• LangChain
• CrewAI
• Zapier AI
• n8n
• Make

Choose based on your technical skills,not hype.

4. Define inputs, outputs, and tools. Every AI agent needs context.

Give it:
• The data it should receive
• The result it should produce
• The tools it can access

Examples:
✓ Google Drive
✓ CRM
✓ Email
✓ Slack
✓ Databases
✓ APIs
✓ Web search
An AI without tools is just a chatbot.
5. Give the agent a clear job description.
Instead of saying:

"Help me."

Say:

"You are a customer support assistant for a luxury hospitality brand. Your role is to answer guest queries, recommend room categories, and escalate complaints when required."

Specific prompts produce better decisions.

6. Add memory.

Good AI remembers.
Store:
• Previous conversations
• Customer preferences
• Business rules
• Company knowledge
• Historical decisions
Memory transforms isolated responses into intelligent assistance.

7. Add guardrails.

Never let AI operate without boundaries.
Define:
• What it can do
• What it cannot do
• When human approval is required
• Security and privacy rules
• Escalation conditions
Reliable AI is controlled AI.

8. Build a simple interface.

Your users shouldn't need technical knowledge.

A simple web page, Slack bot, Teams integration, or internal dashboard is often enough.

If people won't use it, the AI has no business value.

9. Test with real scenarios.

Don't ask:
"Does it work?"
Ask:

• What happens when information is missing?
• What if the user asks something unexpected?
• Does it recover from mistakes?
• Can it explain its reasoning?
• Does it consistently produce useful results?
Production-ready AI is built through iteration, not the first prompt.

The biggest misconception about AI agents is that they're magical.
